conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby. Over the next few minutes we’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s just 10 gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past week; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise or there’s an immediate safety concern. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions together at your pace.

To start: in the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when life with the baby gets a little chaotic?

Sometimes… I can still laugh, but it feels like I have to work harder to find that lighter side. Like the other night, when the baby spit up all over my husband’s shirt—I chuckled, but the laugh kind of fizzled out quickly and I went right back to worrying about whether she was eating enough.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mm… not as much as I used to. I’ll smile if something’s genuinely silly, but it doesn’t come easily—more like “okay, that’s funny” instead of really laughing. Most of the day I’m just tired or focused on the baby, so the laughter feels kind of far away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk—but they’re pretty short-lived. Mostly I’m just thinking ahead to the next feeding or whether the baby will sleep, so the enjoyment feels kind of muted.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m missing some cue or not doing the routine right. Rationally I know babies just have off days, but in the moment my mind jumps to “I must be messing this up somehow.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart races out of nowhere—like when she’s quietly napping and I suddenly need to check the baby monitor three times just to be sure she’s still breathing. I know it sounds silly, but I can’t shake the “what-if” loop even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

It’s happened a couple of times—mostly at night. I’ll be feeding her in the dark and suddenly feel this rush of dread, like something bad is about to happen, even though we’re safe in the house and she’s perfectly fine. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m just one tiny step ahead of the mess. I’ll finally get her down for a nap, look around at the dishes and the laundry, and think, “I’ll never catch up.” I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I’m wading through thick water all the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—just restless. I lie there listening for every squeak from the crib, replaying the day in my head, wondering if I burped her long enough or if that weird rash on her tummy is normal. Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, even when she’s already out cold.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I get waves of it, mostly in the evenings. It’s not all day, but I’ll suddenly feel heavy, like I’m missing something or just empty inside. It usually passes if I talk to my husband or hold the baby, but those gloomy spells catch me off guard.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I got a little teary on Tuesday when she wouldn’t latch and I was running on three hours of sleep, but it didn’t turn into a full cry—more like frustrated, exhausted tears that stopped once she finally nursed and dozed off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be the mom my daughter needs.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire, 3 wks post-delivery

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: diminished laughter, enjoyment “muted”  
- Persistent low mood with evening “waves” of sadness/emptiness  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant care  
- Unwarranted anxiety: somatic tension, “what-if” rumination, repeated monitor-checking  
- Episodic nocturnal panic (rush of dread, shakiness)  
- Subjective overwhelm: “wading through thick water,” sense of never catching up  
- Initial insomnia secondary to hyper-vigilance and rumination  
- Mild lachrymosity when fatigued (no full crying spells)  

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms, predominantly evenings/nights, functionally impairing rest and sense of competence; no anhedonia complete absences, no self-harm ideation.

Risk flags  
- Sleep loss linked to mood and anxiety  
- Recurrent guilt / self-criticism  
- Panic-like surges without environmental trigger  
- Denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts (safety factor)

Screening impression  
Findings suggest clinically significant postpartum distress meeting threshold for further evaluation (possible PPD ± comorbid anxiety); safety risk low at present; recommend formal assessment with standardized EPDS and differential for GAD, adjustment disorder. No immediate safety concerns.
